purpose: Enasidenib is used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in adults whose cancer has come back or has not responded to other treatments. It specifically works for people whose cancer has a certain gene change called an IDH2 mutation. Your doctor will test for this mutation before starting this medicine.
how_it_works: In some people with AML, a gene called IDH2 is mutated, which causes abnormal blood cells to build up and not mature properly. Enasidenib blocks the abnormal IDH2 protein, which helps those immature blood cells grow up into normal, healthy blood cells. Think of it like flipping a switch that helps stuck cells finally finish developing the way they should.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, and feeling tired. You may also notice changes in your blood calcium, potassium, or bilirubin levels. Some patients experience a yellowing of the skin or eyes due to elevated bilirubin, so let your doctor know right away if you notice that.
warnings: A serious and potentially life-threatening condition called differentiation syndrome can occur, especially in the first few months of treatment. Symptoms include fever, trouble breathing, low blood pressure, swelling, or rapid weight gain — call your doctor or go to the emergency room immediately if these happen. This medicine can also harm an unborn baby, so effective birth control is very important during treatment and for at least 2 months after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 100 mg taken by mouth once a day, with or without food. Try to take it at the same time each day. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day, but skip it if it is almost time for your next dose — never double up.
